Did you observe this problem that in certain municipalities there were no prosecutor's offices or regular courts because no one had been appointed to those posts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I touched on this in part when answering your previous questions. The situation on the ground was such that the courts had not been set up, or they were not fully staffed, so that criminal reports kept piling up. Let me just mention that in the course of the work of the MUP, we would not only file a criminal report, we had to follow-up and monitor the outcome. This was important for us to achieve results, and at that time it was not possible. It wasn't just impossible to monitor the outcome, but it was impossible to file the reports because there were no courts in many places.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So let's scroll down, or, rather, let's look at the bottom of the page where it says Ilijas. Where it says that two crimes against civilians had been recorded. In the introductory part, we saw the minister's orders and the forms, and will you agree with me that this is the practical result of those instructions and forms; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Wherever we had such information, there could be no dilemma. We had to act on it ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move down to the last paragraph dealing with Bratunac. Bratunac had the same problem because the court and the Prosecutor's Office were not functioning either in Bratunac or in Srebrenica. You knew about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in English we have to go to the previous page. We need Pale, Novo Sarajevo, and Sarajevo. Is this it? So we have to go back in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you have the Novo Sarajevo Public Security Station and two crimes against the civilian population reported here; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We won't comment, but let's go through the statistics and then I'll show you a document. So this is about war crimes, and we have here reports of war crimes against the civilian population. This is in the centre. Can you remember this? I'll jog your memory with a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I didn't catch when you were showing this document where exactly it says that the crimes reported are classified as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it at the top of the page, Your Honour, about the Sarajevo station. It says two crimes -- two war crimes against civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, in the next paragraph it says in the Stari Grad, Vogosca, Zvornik, Skelani, Orlovo, Hadzici, Rajlovac, and Kula SJBs, we have no information on the number of crimes recorded. Do you know why this information did not arrive before this document was drafted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that question in part, but I can only give you my opinion. Our communications did not always function properly, and I think my colleague, if he has an opportunity, will be able to say more about it, my colleague who worked on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm asking you now to the extent that you can assist. In the next paragraph - I don't know if it's on the same page in English - it says as regards the non-functioning of courts and prosecutor's offices on the territories of the municipalities of Bratunac, Skelani, Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica, and Ilijas, so there are not a few municipalities where the prosecutor's office and the courts were not functioning; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubts about that. I said that. But I may have understood your previous question from another angle, which is why I said my colleague would be able to say more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And at the end of page 2, the author of the document orders all the stations to immediately submit criminal reports in spite of all this and to provide information about this immediately. So you have to monitor the situation in the judiciary, and as soon as a court is established, you have to submit and file your criminal reports. Is that the correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is correct. It's what I've just said, monitoring the outcome of criminal proceedings. That was our duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, just one question before you move on. The two war crimes committed against the civilian population that were registered in respect of Sarajevo which you showed to us just a while ago, I wonder if there's any information about the victims of these two war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next document will provide the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, is this information coming from your Sarajevo Centre of Public Security to the municipal stations; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can confirm this statistical information because you are familiar with it; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, at that time when we exchanged information, and when I look at this it jogs my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as the chief of the centre is no longer alive, I think this is the best witness through whom to tender this document, so I now wish to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we see the last page of it, please. Is it Mr. Cvijetic who has -- who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same problem that Ms. Korner had with the document yesterday. It's a public document; we had a similar problem yesterday. But there is no doubt in the witness's mind that this information comes from the Sarajevo CJB; however, we don't have the last page in electronic form. We looked for it, but we couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the front page for a moment, because I can't find it in the bundle I was given. I agree, the document I had did say it was from the CSB; this just says information about the crime prevention measures on the territory; however it does cover the area, so I have no objection to the document going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit 1D188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document 1D00-5229.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. Your Honours, it was added later. It's not in the binder. We have to look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask the usher to give this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, here we have a specific criminal report for a specific crime. From the description of the crime, we see that the person reported, Stanko Knezevic, was a guard at the penitentiary Kula, and when 12 prisoners were taken outside to the hill called Zuc where they were digging trenches, and when they were brought back in, he lined them up, opened fire at them from an automatic weapon, and then approached those who were still living and killed them off. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is an example for several purposes. In this case, there is no question of whether it is a war crime or not. The police who filed this report, the police station of Vogosca under the new chief because the previous one had been suspended, qualifies these acts in the preamble as a war crime against prisoners of war. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thus, in such cases even the police had no dilemma. They had a specific perpetrator to deal with; the perpetrator was identified. And on the same day, the day of the crime, he was already in custody. The report was filed and submitted to the relevant prosecutor's office in Sarajevo. In such cases, it was the military authorities who had jurisdiction, but you could also get involved if you apprehended such a perpetrator. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should just clarify why the Military Prosecutor's Office was the recipient of this criminal report, because, at the time, this person was a military conscript. The crime was heinous, and we acted promptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Promptly, that means quickly, urgently, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness is aware of this case and in the context of our discussion about the prosecution of war crimes, I believe the document is relevant for our Defence and also for the Trial Chamber perhaps, so I tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit 1D189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like briefly to tackle the topic of the disbanding of the so-called special units to see how the minister's orders were executed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's call up 65 ter 2677. I'm sorry, 2677. Tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you have it? Have you found it? Mr. Borovcanin, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number is it in my binder?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told it's already exhibited. So it's P827. Sorry, 857.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Vlasenica station says that a unit like that existed. It had been set up just before the war started. You already talked about that period when no control was possible. But it also says that the minister's order must be obeyed, and he explains how. A part was transferred to the reserve force and another part was placed under military command. First of all, do you know about this document; and, second, do you know about this unit that was disbanded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it falls under my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the answer is yes on both counts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've talked about it in my answers to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that all the requirements are met for receiving this document. Oh, no, I apologise, it's already an exhibit. May I now ask for 65 ter 1266. It's actually P731. It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Your tab 53.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Rogatica Public Security Station, 14 August 1992. Rogatica is sending this report to your centre, and they write in paragraph 1 that there are no longer any problems caused by paramilitary formations and their activity. But in the fourth paragraph, the large one, it says that all members of the police station had been engaged in the military and the station was totally unable to work, all 36 men. In the middle of the paragraph, there's a sentence that begins with the words: "In the said period, there were constant attempts to subordinate the employees of SJB Rogatica, first to the Territorial Defence, and later to the Army of the SRBH, which created problems among our employees at the beginning, because they had been given information that a kind of military administration was introduced and that the Ministry of Interior, including SJBs, should not operate during the war at all." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the ambitions of the military authorities to suborn the police to them completely. Is this one example in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there are only one or two stations where this did not occur. There was a pronounced duality on the part of the army, if I can put it that way, because they always seem to think that we were shirking military duty, and they were hindering our regular police work in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The last sentence confirms what you say, the chief says that he managed to win a halfway solution, that is, to have at least 50 per cent of his personnel remain at the station while another 50 per cent is going to take part in combat. You see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the last paragraph, the sentence that begins with problems regarding treatment of prisoners. Read that through. The chief is actually echoing what you said a moment ago. The civilian population from war-affected areas are brought to safety by the army, but then nobody takes care of them. And then he says, Although such persons did not fall under our jurisdiction pursuant to the Law on Internal Affairs, we guarded those people and organised their transfer to territories controlled by the authorities of the former BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn the page both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You see what the chief is saying: "We were unable to grant these citizens free movement because we could not guarantee their safety, in view of the fact that the entire area of Rogatica was engulfed in military activity." Sir, this confirms what you were saying about this problem that was new to the police, and you were looking for solutions as you went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I discussed that with the Prosecutor. I tried to explain. This was a long-running problem. We were left holding the baby. We had to take care of these people with whom we were stuck, and we had to organise transportation because there was no other solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told this document is already an exhibit, so we can move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll deal very briefly with the topic of the removal of persons who had a criminal record or who were under prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call 65 ter 2884.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tab 46.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it on the screen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Vlasenica Public Security Station reports that he had taken steps - as he says in the first paragraph - all kinds of legal and disciplinary measures against the employees, both active and reserve, whenever there is evidence of a breach of disciplinary or other duty. And in paragraph 2, we see how many criminal reports had been filed against the staff of the station and for which crimes. And reserve policemen were simply dismissed. Further below, he talks about the measures taken against active-duty policemen, regular police officers. Mr. Borovcanin, you knew the chief of this station, and it seems from this document that he was rather diligent in carrying out the minister's order, is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Djuric. I can say very briefly that he was one of our best men. A very serious man, very conscious of the law, and dedicated in law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to see his reports and statistics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rather, should I say, servile or helpful whenever we would come for an inspection visit. In some other places, people would try to stash away documents; but, no, in this station, everything was readily given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you were aware of these statistics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that this document qualifies to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit 1D190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next document is from the 65 ter list, 2811.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tab 41.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Will you just confirm for me that a month later the same chief continues the same activity? And look at the next -- at the second paragraph, eight criminal reports, 47 members removed. The man is obviously purging his police station.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. It's self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is the man whom you described as very diligent in doing his job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very diligent indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document for admission for the same reasons as the one before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, for this document and the previous document, I have the difficulty that I fail to see the relevance of it. Both documents seem to show that in these two police stations, the chiefs were diligent in ensuring that the policemen working there were acting correctly and if they did not perform their duties according to the book, they would be met by disciplinary sanctions. That seems to show that the police station was working well and that the chiefs of the police stations were eager to ensure that the employees were acting correctly. But just how is this relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is very relevant. If Mr. Stanisic is charged with failing to take appropriate steps and that by omission he allowed crimes to be committed at police stations and he allowed official authority to be abused, then it's certainly relevant to show that he had taken all the steps to enforce his measures using all the mechanisms at his disposal, and he made those mechanisms work. That is the purpose of my questioning and these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that very well. But still, I find it's of little assistance to this trial if what we are being told here is only that ordinary civilian crimes, if I may call it that, that is to say, not war crimes, were investigated and prosecuted. The evidence that you are offering to us would have been far more relevant to the case if you were able to show that indeed war crimes were being prosecuted diligently. But apart from the two war crimes that we saw committed in Sarajevo five or six documents ago, nothing in the present document or the previous document tends to show that there was much interest in prosecuting the war crimes and the crimes against humanity for which your client is charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're wrong. It's not only the statistics. I have showed to you a specific criminal report for a war crime, and I discussed this issue with the witness yesterday. Namely, that even in these traditional general crimes, especially murders, it is possible to find cases involving a national element that are qualified initially as a murder. But it is up to the prosecutor to give the final legal qualification. So it's premature on the basis of the first step, which is the criminal report, to say whether it ultimately ended up as a war crime or not. I just wanted to show the good intent to fight all forms of serious crime and that there was no discrimination whatsoever in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That doesn't help me much in relation to the last two documents, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I tender this document on the same grounds as before, I want to add something in response to Judge Harhoff. Namely, the minister of the interior is obliged to create the proper conditions for the ministry to work in strict keeping with the law; and to prosecute war crimes, among other things. And in order to provide the right conditions, and to ensure that there are mechanisms in place, and to lend authority to the officers who are to prosecute all crimes including war crimes, the minister first has to purge the personnel and recreate the ministry, remove people who do not want to work and who obstruct the work and the orders of the minister. That is why this document is relevant, and that's why I propose it for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit 1D191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, Mr. Stanisic stopped being minister in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who took his place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Ratko Adzic, but I can't be sure. You really took me aback with that question, because the ministers changed very quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the next minister continue with these efforts and these investigations, because you were still in your job? In all the areas that we've been discussing these past days, did you continue to feel the progress and improvement in the work of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we professional people were very disappointed when Mr. Stanisic left his post. I cannot remember clearly his immediate successor, but the series of ministers later either did not know anything about the professional aspects of the work, or they were simply appointees from above and not people who knew the trade. In any case, we had loads of problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: With the return of Mr. Stanisic in 1994, were some of these scandals from 1992 taken up again, and did investigations restart?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware in particular of the scandal with the theft of these Volkswagon Golfs, and I know Mr. Stanisic as someone who simply doesn't let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In 1994, there was a very big financial scandal involving some 10 million Deutschemark intended for the purpose of petrol for Republika Srpska. This contract landed in the lap of cabinet ministers who are at the same time owners of private companies. And then suddenly there was no money and no petrol. Do you know that Mr. Stanisic started investigations against a large number of cabinet ministers and said in public in the press that he would pursue them to the bitter end, whatever that cost? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I remember. And that was a scandal; that's the proper word to use, "scandal," which really upset people. Imagine fighters at the front line hearing something like this. It was taken up by members of the Assembly. There were complaints by many people asking us, Are you going to see this through? There were others who were not very happy with this manner of working. And with some small reservations, this is my personal opinion, I can say that Mr. Stanisic was getting in people's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic was criticised by the top leadership for making this scandal public. There was another scandal concerning aluminium and so on. And do you know that after that he was forced to resign?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know about this. And these are major issues. When he saw that he did not have the support he needed, I'm not surprised that he resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And my last question: How did you professional policemen respond to his resignation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what the police are like. When someone is strong and persistent, sometimes policemen don't like that. But if you look at the ultimate goal of establishing a proper police force, we did not like this. We knew who we had, but we didn't know who was to come. And there were many problems as transpired later on, but that's a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Borovcanin, thank you. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have completed my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, for this delay. Mr. Cvijetic finished sooner than I expected him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Borovcanin. My name is Dragan Krgovic. We have already met. We met briefly a few days ago. I appear on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin. And, on his behalf, I will put a few questions to you concerning your testimony. I will touch on a topic addressed by Mr. Cvijetic briefly. You were shown a number of documents which you commented on concerning disciplinary responsibility of MUP employees. From the documents which I saw and from your responses, it follows that the procedure needed to dismiss someone and carry out disciplinary proceedings, in line with the legislation and rules, that this was quite an arduous procedure, time consuming procedure in fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. One needed time to document something properly. It would have been dishonourable to take measures without evidence and with out carrying the procedure out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So that some of these cases ended years after the initial violation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were going through a chaotic time, and that's why it took so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were aware of the practice that, in compliance with the minister's instructions, as regards cleaning up the police, people in authority used a so-called summary version or short version of the procedure; and when they heard that someone was not doing his job properly, they would send them over to the ministry -- or to the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if we thought that we would put someone at the disposal of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And taking someone off the police roster would mean that that person had been dismissed, in fact. That this was some sort of disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was an active-duty policeman and if he was suspected of a crime, he would have to go through criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings; however, if he was a reservist, he would be taken off the list immediately because he was at the wrong place and he would be put at the disposal of the army. And if someone had committed a crime on the territory of the police, a criminal report would be filed. That was the proper road to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the dismissal from one's job was the most severe measure that could be taken in disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the ultimate measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you take a reserve policeman off the roster and hand him over to the Ministry of Defence, his employment in the police is terminated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only one thing changes; his military deployment is not with us, but with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when a reserve policeman was in question, the best way to remove him from the police and the fastest way was to send him over to the military; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was, to avoid them giving a bad example to other policemen both active duty and reservists. One couldn't wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because, in fact, the biggest problem in the police were not regular policemen who had become police officers through the regular procedure. It was these reserve policemen who, due to circumstances, had become members of the reserve forces of the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to understand this properly, many people who became members of the reserve police force thought that they would have an easier time there, while, at the same time, those who were hesitant or prone to criminal activities thought that the uniform would give them a sort of cover and help them undertake their criminal activities. They were very upset when we decided to send them over to the army. In Novo Sarajevo about 400 of them blocked the police station and didn't allow the local chief to go in or out, or the other senior officers in that station. I arrived there and tried to talk to them. Some of them were drunk; they were carrying automatic weapons; and thanks to my experience, because I believe I am able to communicate with people, I choose my words carefully because the situation was very volatile, I managed to get them to disperse peacefully. But I do want to stress that in the end the decision was complied with and they were all put at the disposal of the Army of the Republika Srpska. And that's just one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When we look at the statistics, when we look at the report you discussed with Mr. Cvijetic containing the number of MUP members who were prosecuted and who -- against whom disciplinary procedures were instituted and who were dismissed, we have to add the reservists to that number who were taken off the roster; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you look at the reports arriving from certain SJBs containing the numbers of people, of men, officers against whom proceedings have been instituted, whether criminal or disciplinary, to that number one should also add those who have been taken off the roster in the reserve police force and put at the disposal of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because, at that time, our members were on our roster. I didn't understand your question at first, but yes, yes, you are quite right. There's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now move on to another topic you spoke about, that the Prosecutor asked you about. The Prosecutor asked you some questions including one about identifying the voices of certain people. You heard some intercepts, and you spoke about several persons whose voices you recognised. I'd like to take you back to another intercept that was not put to you during the examination-in-chief, but it was put to you during your interview. You will remember that the Prosecutor showed you a document. It's 65 ter 1056. You will see it on the monitor, but if it's easier for you, you can look at the hard copy if the usher will hand it to you. That's marked for identification 5981.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's in the binder. It's in his binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- do you see it? Do you see it on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This transcript was shown to you, and you also heard the recording of this intercept, so you looked at the transcript while listening to the recording; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was during my first interview in 2007. That's precisely what happened. Mr. Nasiri [phoen], I think, was the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you told the Prosecutor on that occasion that you might be able to recognise Stanisic's voice but not Stojan's voice, and you hadn't had all that many contacts with Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Stojan's voice is one I wouldn't be able to recognise. There was a Gvozden whose name -- whose voice I couldn't recognise, but I could recognise Mico's voice. And the other voices, well, sometimes if you don't see the speaker, you can't really be sure whose voice it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the fact that the recording was played to you and that the transcript was shown to you, this helped you identify the speakers, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the practice is a little unusual, isn't it, if you're being asked to identify a voice while being shown a transcript where that person's name is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the rules. I thought that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, you were shown -- you were asked about a meeting in Belgrade on the 11th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court the minutes of that meeting; that's P160. That's page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the first page of that document and now let's look at page 3. Look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court that's the page with ERN 0324-1851.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify. You see that the opening remarks are made by Mico Stanisic as the minister, which is quite normal; it's to be expected, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the next page where the discussion is summarised - 0324-1852, that's the next page - it says here, Summary of the discussion. So this is only a summary, as far as I was able to see, of all the interventions, but it doesn't mean that the speaker spoke in this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whoever drew up the minutes just summarised this in any way they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You don't recall the order in which the participants spoke?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what I'm interested in now is on page 5 in the B/C/S version and page 8 in the English version. So could we please have that page shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, look at the fourth paragraph from the bottom on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please. Page 5. ERN 0324-1855.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I'm still looking at the summary. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, the next page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it will turn up. Just a wait a little. You see it's the longest paragraph, the one in the middle which says "due to the loss ..." or "because of the casualties..." I will read you a sentence which is not clear in the English translation where

utterances.speaker: MR. ZUPLJANIN SAYS
utterances.text: "The army is asking for the engagement of the entire composition to be resubordinated and then they are pushing them forward on to the most difficult front lines. This should be -- this should be made impossible. Should be prevented." In your responses, you spoke about resubordination. Did they ask for the entire personnel of the station to be resubordinated to them and engaged in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that as follows: This tendency could be seen on the territory of the centre also, and at the meeting I learned that that's how it was in the Krajina. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are almost at the end of this session, I think we could take a break now and continue later on so the witness can recover from his cough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask, are we in Court I this afternoon? Are we in Court I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we are in this courtroom at 2.15. We aren't going to rise immediately. Mr. Borovcanin, the usher will escort you from the courtroom now, but we will resume here at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will raise two matters on which it is seeking submissions. On Friday, the 19th of February, the Prosecutor informed the parties and the Chamber by e-mail of a document that is intends to use with Mr. Borovcanin. Among these documents was Rule 65 ter 1931. This document was tendered by the Prosecution yesterday and admitted into evidence as P998. It has come to the Chamber's attention that Rule 65 ter 1931 does not appear on the Prosecution's exhibit list submitted on the 8th of June, 2009, nor is it included in the Prosecution's motion of Thursday, 18th February, to amend the exhibit list. The Chamber asks the Prosecution for an explanation when the hearing resumes at 14.15. Second matter is the following: On the 22nd February, the Prosecution informed the parties and the Chamber by e-mail of the documents it intends to use with ST-166, who begins testimony tomorrow. Twenty one of these documents are subject of the Prosecution's motion of the 18th of February to amend its exhibit list. These are Rule 65 ter numbers 03500 to 03520. The Trial Chamber has also noted that two other documents which Prosecution -- which the Prosecution intends to use with ST-166 are also subject of the motion. These are Rule 65 ter numbers 03557 and 03559. The Trial Chamber intends to rule on the motion in respect of those 23 documents before ST-166 begins to testify. The Stanisic Defence responded on the 23rd of February opposing the addition. However, the Zupljanin Defence has not yet responded. Mr. Pantelic, if you intend to respond to the motion regarding the 23 documents or the motion in its entirety, the Trial Chamber will hear you as we resume at 14.15 hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours want me to deal with the exhibit now or after the witness is finished? 1931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: After, please. After.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at this applies to me also because these are housekeeping matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Borovcanin, we were at this document which I would kindly ask to be brought up on the screen again. It is document 560. P160, I apologise. It is page number 5 in the B/C/S version and page number 8 in the English version. This is the page with the ERN 0324-1855 in the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, we have talked about this part, we talked about it before the break, about this practice for entire police stations to be resubordinated to the army so that the police stations would actually be depleted of personnel and would not be able to do their own work. That was a large-scale phenomenon, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were talking about the functioning of the MUP about the various rules and regulations, the way it should be organised, and the way in which it should function and proceed generally, you were speaking from the aspect, shall we say, of a normal state of affairs, normal times, as it were. But for one to appreciate the situation in which you were concretely at that time and the entire MUP, that should be placed within a war context, should it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In May or April in 1992, nothing was normal. The situation was chaotic. First of all, it was difficult for one to observe everything and to see what was happening, let alone take the necessary measures. One had to be mindful of one's sequence of steps. To be able to take any steps, one had to be aware of what was happening. One had to have the proper information. Everything was taken in one stride.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is much easier, you will agree with me, for us to observe the functioning of the MUP in that period from this time distance and to also find fault with it than it was for you who were right there in the thick of the events and when you should have been the ones to be best informed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, of course, when some time has elapsed, if you observe things after a distance, after the passage of time, with a sober head, you, of course, in hindsight, know what measures should have been taken. But one has to conjure up the situation that we had, this picture of chaos. It is very difficult for someone who was not there, who had not experienced it himself. And, of course, that being so, it is easy to criticise in hindsight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it is the united stand of all the participants in 1992 that the situation was all but satisfactory and that actually at that meeting you came to actually air your troubles to one another and to see what could be done; was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I spoke before about this topic, I said it was first of all an occasion for us to meet and to see one another and then it was easier for us when we realised that problems were also present in other areas, that they were common problems. That is when we could actually set about making a strategy to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And more or less the problems which were presented at this meeting that Stojan Zupljanin speaks about, these problems also featured throughout the territory of Republika Srpska, including your own centre of public security; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already talked about the centre. We heard about it from Mr. Stojan and from Mr. Savic in respect of Trebinje and other centres in Doboj, et cetera. We all realised -- altogether realised how formidable the problems were that we were all faced with and that we had to set about dealing with those problems within the MUP in an organised way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said, actually, Mr. Zupljanin, Stojan Zupljanin is talking about the existence of certain centres and places where the army or actually the Crisis Staffs were bringing the civilian population and handing it over like a hot potato to the MUP. That is the first time that you heard of such things happening, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first information that we received about such events at that collegium meeting, at least as far as I'm concerned, that was the first time I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your interview with the Prosecutor, you said that -- I shall paraphrase, but the gist of it was that you said, If I had not read this statement, my memory has faded, but I do know something else, namely as a result of this contribution of Stojan Zupljanin's, the ministry took an action. There was a MUP inspection which actually inspected the collection centres in situ, and, after that, they were disbanded. Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The first information about this -- after receiving the first information about this, the minister took urgent and prompt action because he was aware of how prejudicial this generally was, and he ordered that all these centres within the Banja Luka centre area should be inspected and proper action taken, which was indeed done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because bearing in mind what Stojan Zupljanin has presented that it was actually the army and the Crisis Staffs in the various municipalities, that they were the ones setting up these collection centres. This was not something that could be dealt with by individual police action. It had to be on a more general level, the government, the army, the minister who was the one to initiate the resolution of that problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my -- what little I know about this, and as I said before, any war in the world also produces prisoners of war; that is one of the collateral damages of war. So my modest knowledge, as I said according to the Law on All People's Defence, the Army of the Republika Srpska was primarily responsible for the collection centres, for their security, for their reporting to the ICRS, et cetera. Members of the ministry - but I didn't know that at the time - in Krajina, they asked us to secure these camps; so it was indeed a hot potato that was given us in that sense. And it should be seen as such, because it was primarily the responsibility of the army. It was within their competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the information given by Stojan Zupljanin at this extended collegium about the existence of these centres and the conditions which obtained there, as well as the subsequent action the minister took including -- involving you, this is something -- this is something that anyone would have done including you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, first of all, they would point out the problem, if any existed. That is the first step. And this information opened the eyes of us all. We started re-examining what was happening in our area, as I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And an adequate reaction on the part of the minister ensued, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was something that broke to no delay. This was the priority of priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, after that, the ministry sent numerous dispatches and instructions on what kind of action was taken in cases like this, what was to be done. So action was -- some action taken, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not just call it an action. Action is something very specific or maybe a one-time phenomenon. This was a series of measures and activities. First of all, by the preparation of dispatches informing the competent centres, the SJBs, et cetera. And in every dispatch, it was insisted that the content, i.e., the orders given from the top of the MUP, should be executed. This was done in continuity. This was arduous work. And that is how it should be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 6 in the Serbian version, and in English it's page 9. It's 0324-1856. The -- well, it's page 8, actually, in the English version; that's where the answer starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, look at the second paragraph from the top where Mr. Zupljanin talks about the problems you mentioned today, several thousand court cases pending, no judges to try criminal cases, intimidation of judges, courts not functioning at all in some areas. So this is the same sort of situation that obtained on the territory of your centre, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another problem, as I understand this, hardened criminals are being released from prison, and this is hindering the establishment of the rule of law. As I understand this, the police would arrest someone against whom a criminal report had been filed, and then they would release him and he would turn up somewhere else. And, of course, this influenced your work and your ability to prevent crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you've jogged my memory and reminded me of a problem which was a huge problem in practice. We would bring someone in, detain him while we did our operative work. We couldn't hold that person for longer than three days. We would ostensibly file a criminal report, but there was no one to hand it over to, and that person would be at liberty again. And very often we would get complaints from citizens. They would say, How come this person is at large, wandering around, firing shots, threatening people. But, I tell you, it was a long process, and that's how it should be understood. Let me assure you, and I'm not speaking only from the viewpoint of the Serbian MUP, it was probably like that in the Federation as well. Criminals took over in many areas. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Zupljanin, there was mention of the way the MUP was funded, and it was concluded that the MUP should be funded from a single centre because local municipalities who funded MUP stations thought this gave them the right to issue orders, and this had an impact on the proper workings of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already told you, this was an enormous problem. If someone is paying me, then I answer to them, metaphorically speaking. However, this was a mistake on the part of people who thought they could now have their own private police force. This couldn't be allowed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the general standpoint was that all these issues should be solved, that conclusions should be drawn up, and that efforts should be made to put a stop to all this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was a significant new beginning in the organisation of the MUP and its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, to the best of your knowledge, in the further work of the MUP, everything possible was done to create a foundation for the MUP, appropriate to a state governed by the rule of law, and to establish a proper hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In every government there are some ministries which are the most important, and among them is always the Ministry of the Interior which is in charge of maintaining law and order, protecting citizens and their property. With all due respect to other institutions, especially in times such as those were, the MUP was an institution which had to have support at all levels in order for it to be what it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, certainly, in your later work, you saw that there was a lot of resistance coming from various sides, that it was a long and arduous process, and that up to the end of 1992 it was very difficult to establish order; some sort of order was established, but not fully?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was difficult. I have to make just a small digression and tell you that in that period I was more afraid of my own Serbs, so to speak, because of the operative action I had to take on the ground to prevent their criminal activities, than I was afraid of being killed on a front line somewhere. And I wasn't the only one. We were all threatened. We mentioned paramilitaries and other self-organised criminal groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this period, that is, April, May, June, and July up to this meeting, complete chaos prevailed, disorganisation, and it was not possible for the MUP to carry out its work properly and according to the law. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course that's how it was. A lot of things were not functioning. Communications were not functioning. It's a long story. I do not want to take up your time, but that's really how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Borovcanin, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, I thought we'd actually dealt with communications because we looked at the report. Is it your -- now your evidence that between April and July there was no communication between the CSB and the SJBs? Because that's what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in several places. But if you were to take the context of everything I said about the functioning of communications, I think the real conclusion would be that in some places it was very difficult at the beginning. I never said it did not function at all, but it was all work in progress. We didn't have staff; we had to find lads who could install things. We had some ancient Motorolas, museum pieces. And you have to understand that, unlike many other centres, we sprang up from scratch. We entered premises not belonging to us to start work, communications were difficult, and I said that we even had to organise a courier service when needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I accept entirely that communication was difficult, but it is not your evidence, I just want to make this quite clear, is that right, that there was no communication, that, in other words, that SJBs were wholly cut off from the CSB in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point they were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April. April and part of May. And there were some with whom we had no communication whatsoever. But for me to remember out of those 25 stations under our jurisdiction, I'd have to give it a lot of thought to recall how things happened and how we managed to cover all these communications. It would take time for me to clarify it. I know exactly how things went.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would it -- let's see if we can arrive at a happy medium. Would this be fair: From time to time there would be difficulties in communication with a particular SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at things in that narrow way, throughout the war there are occasional difficulties in communication, but, generally speaking, the beginning was very difficult. At the beginning, there were more times when communications were cut off than when they were working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Telephone lines were all existing, even during April and May, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To illustrate or to help you understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't want an illustration. I want you tell me, please, when you say telephone lines were not working between the CSB and the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war all communications were cut off, even in the security centre where we were, there was only a single telephone line. I don't know how it functioned. I'm not an expert, but that was the only communication we had with the federal part of town. And if I were now to start talking about Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza, and so on, that's the western part of Sarajevo, I don't know when was the first time I established communication. I can't recall, but it was certainly not in April or May, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying you had absolutely no communication with Vogosca, Ilijas, and Ilidza for the whole of April and the whole of May? No reports, nothing. Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that for the entire two months there was nothing at all. I can't remember every detail. But, certainly, lines were very difficult. The technicians in charge did their best to set it up. But, well, really I don't understand your question. I'm trying to give you as objective an answer as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a very simple question. I don't know what the difficulty is. But I think you've dealt with it, in any event. All right, I want to go back to some of the matters you were asked about during cross-examination. Firstly, you were shown a document which, just a moment, I think had 65 ter number 2398. No, I think it's P993. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we have in English the second page, please, because this was the part that you were shown. It's in B/C/S also, the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about this by Mr. Cvijetic, paragraph in the middle, about the appointment of Mr. Stevanovic and Vasiljevic and about the appointment by some other people, by the municipal bodies. Right. And you then said -- you agreed, when it was put to you by Mr. Cvijetic, that there was a lot of interference by the local bodies. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked, weren't you, during the course of your interview about this, about interference by Crisis Staffs. And I'd like you to refresh your memory, if you could, to what you told the investigators.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you referring to the 2007 interview or the one I had with you before appearing in the courtroom? Which particular interview are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't have an interview with me, but you had an interview, one interview, and one interview only in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, there is in fact, Your Honours a B/C/S -- it's one of the few; we've had it translated, amazingly enough, into B/C/S. And the Defence put it into their document bundle. And I think you'll find it -- well, I don't know, it might -- we didn't have any dividers given to us, so I don't know where it was put in. Maybe the Defence can help. There is a B/C/S version of his interview, and it's page 30 of 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are referring to the interview or the tape of the interview, it is in the witness's binder under number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be a copy in the witness's own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it. I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good. Could you turn to page -- at the bottom you'll see it's got page numbers. And it says page 30 of 77. And could you just read to yourself from halfway -- from the question about halfway down the page and then for the next couple of pages. So pages 30, 31, and 32. Let me know when you've finished, please. Let me know when you've read down to the answer -- or the question from Mr. Nasir [phoen]. You said that the Crisis Staff had no influence on your work as a police chief or the CSB chief of police affairs, and you said, Absolutely not. Just let me know when you have reached that part.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm done. You can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Having refreshed your memory from this interview, is it right that you told the investigators on three occasions that there had been no complaints to you from SJB chiefs about influence from Crisis Staffs and indeed they had no effect on your work as a police chief. Now you seem to say that the opposite is the case; that the authorities, the municipal authorities were interfering, interfering constantly. So which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to prevent a misquote, the interview refers to the Crisis Staff. And in his report, the gentleman said that municipal bodies were doing -- making some appointments in the SJB and that is what led to the duality. So in his interview he is referring to a different agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly the question I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said, In your interview you told them that the Crisis Staffs had no effect on your work or nor did the SJB chiefs complain to you that. Now you're saying municipal authorities were interfering. What's the difference, at this stage we are talking about, between the Crisis Staffs and the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a difficult question, for me to make this distinction between the Crisis Staff and the municipal authorities. I'll tell you why. I know who the municipal authorities were, appointed people, the President of the Assembly of the Executive Board, et cetera. But with their functions overlapped with other posts, that is something that I don't know, namely for a president of the municipality to also have been the president of the Crisis Staff. I don't know that that was the case. I was not affiliated with any party. I have no information about the goings on as far as the Crisis Staffs were concerned. What I do know for a fact is that we had such problems, and I referred to Mr. Cvijetic in connection with Marko Milanovic and a local [indiscernible], shall I call them that, who were actually waging policy at municipal level. That is the whole truth about that. As regards to the interview, let me just say how I understood that things were being done because when I see a document, my memory is jogged. Perhaps when I gave this interview in 2007 I was selectively given some documents for my perusal, and so guided by the documents that were presented before me, that is actually how I remembered specific things. I can understand this as a policeman, this sort of investigative method. Had I been formulated a question differently or shown a different document, perhaps I would have given a different reply, because my replies were guided in this way. This is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just go back to the beginning of it, because the question -- you weren't shown any documents, were you, Mr. Borovcanin? The investigator said to you: "Can you tell us about since you are visiting the SJBs in the 1992, what role the Crisis Staffs had in the workings of the SJB?" So it was an open-ended, no document question. Your answer: "I never had the opportunity to be present at any meeting of that kind, so I cannot officially comment on any of the role, because, personally, did I not see any influence on them within the stations." The investigator said to you: "I understand that. You didn't attend a meeting, but you were meeting -- you were within the police stations. Did they tell you that any influence on Crisis Staffs on them" -- it's rather badly phrased, but ... And your answer, again: "As far as I'm familiar with, no." And then it went on for two pages, as you've just read. So you weren't shown any documents and you never said to them, I'm sorry, I don't know what a Crisis Staff is. You knew what a Crisis Staff was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to put this in simple terms. A Crisis Staff is a sort of a self-organised group of people, that is how I conceived of it. I never attended any of their sessions. That is true. But, by just being there, I learned that a local authorities were interfering with the MUP's personnel policy. I mentioned a certain document -- a certain gentleman at whose place I spent the night, and this is illustrative. This man who had a very good intention of putting things in order who was called the commissioner of town, this was one Lukic, he warned me, because I delved deeper into some crime issues and problems. He told me, Do not go out at night because you will vanish into thin air. And I'm just illustrating because something similar had happened to him. I'm just illustrating the situation at the time. Had the police been different, the things would have been different. And local authorities definitely interfered. It is -- this is not just in relation to the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff cannot explain everything that transpired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, in this particular event that was covered in this report, if we look at the paragraph underneath that, it was suggested and immediately accepted by Ostoja Bozic, that the command of the deputy posts were to be taken over by Bogdan Stevanovic and Milos Vasiljevic who have for these posts the decision of the ministry, and the handover was to be carried out. So once it was discovered what was happening, the proper personnel took over the police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This just confirms that the ministry's endeavours to put things in order. And that is how Mr. Stevanovic and Vasiljevic were appointed. These were experienced policemen, especially Bogdanovic. But it was thanks to a degree of flexibility that we exhibited that we could solve this problem in a peaceful way. The people realised that they had been wrong, and they withdrew peacefully, stepped down peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reality was that the local -- the municipal authorities could suggest appointments, and quite often did, but it was only the minister who had the power to make those appointments, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just omitted to say one thing. Yes, the municipal authorities could suggest it, but they -- the potential candidates had to pass some tests, physical, mental ability, aptitude, and what we call -- what we used to call moral and political suitability of candidates had also to be checked; they had to be vetted for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And on the same note, let's have a look at this Maksimovic saga, shall we. You were shown a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure, I think it was produced as an exhibit, nor am I sure what the number is, but I think it's -- it was 1D00-6682. It's the one after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's the 31st October response from Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, yes. Thank you very much. Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's 1D185.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have that up, sorry. I suppose I didn't make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this, I think, was to demonstrate the interference and the difficulties with this police station, at least I assume it is. And it states there: "The policemen have issued an ultimatum. They will all quit Vogosca if the chiefs goes. He was appointed by the Assembly of the Vogosca, a Serbian municipality, and only that Assembly can recall him."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could we have up, please, 65 ter 3091.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Does that show that Mr. Maksimovic, contrary to what's asserted in this document here, was temporarily assigned the duties and task of commander until the adoption of the rules of procedure of the Ministry of the Interior, and that's dated the 1st of April and signed, stamped anyhow, by Mico Stanisic? Were you aware that he wasn't officially appointed? I know it's temporarily, that was while all of this was going on, as Mr. Stanisic says, that he was appointed by Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was the chief? I knew that. As for this document, this is the first time I see it. And I didn't know that he had been appointed to this post as indicated here. I know that there had been a suggestion, a proposal on behalf of the local community, but the checking here was purely done, this is what I can assess on the basis of this document, prior to the appointment, Mr. Maksimovic's appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are two different posts, different functions. Here he is appointed the commander, the "komandir." It was the municipal -- the competent municipal organ appointed him chief of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can see that it is the commander in the sense of "komandir."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was appointed commander -- I don't know whether the -- wasn't he also -- he couldn't have been the chief of the SJB had he not been authorised as chief of the SJB by Mico Stanisic as minister; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question the way it was put. What do you mean by "he had not been authorised"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Without a formal appointment by Mico Stanisic, could Mr. Maksimovic, whatever the Assembly or the Crisis Staff in Vogosca wanted to do, could he have been the chief of the SJB without an appointment from Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, that is exactly so. I don't know about this intermezzo between his appointment as commander, "komandir," or -- and his later appointment as chief. I can suppose that someone from the local authorities promoted him to the position of chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Let's not repeat this, shall we. Whatever the local authority recommended or wanted to do, they had no power, did they, to appoint the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And this was so in other areas, not only in Vogosca. They did not have the power, but they did appoint. How did they do that? They ignored the MUP as an institution. That is why this interlude is not clear to me, as I say, because they probably appointed him without the knowledge of the minister. Otherwise, the relevant, or whatever, would have been signed by the minister, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well -- all right. For the moment, let's not take that further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic. You were shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you don't want this document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, well, if I can. He says he has never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, if I can, I would, yes. It is definitely on our 65 ter list. Well, Your Honours, I certainly do ask, if there's no objection, if I can have this exhibited. It's obviously relevant to the saga that Mr. Cvijetic has been going through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we object for a very simple reason: The admission of this document has to be accompanied by an explanation, but we no longer have the right to question the witness. How it came about that this Maksimovic became komandir, a commander on a temporary basis, but we will have to deal with that through another witness, because I cannot testify and I can no longer examine this witness. So we'll have to wait for another witness to whom we can put this question in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we'll have it just marked for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1000 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to a slightly different topic but an allied one. You were -- it was put to you by Mr. Cvijetic again that Mico Stanisic repeated his order on a number of occasions about the removal of police who had committed crimes to be put at the disposal of the army. You remember that? Do you have any idea why Mico Stanisic felt it necessary to repeat that order so often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question is simple. Is it logical for members of the MUP to be criminals and to continue working as police officers? That doesn't go together, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but he was the minister of the interior. Why wasn't one order sufficient? Why repeat it? If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary because the thing didn't end with just one crime. Crimes kept being carried out. So every time this happened, he needed to repeat his order and say, Let's clean up our ranks. Just one order wasn't enough to finish the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why didn't -- I understand what you say that this didn't mean that no criminal proceedings would be instituted, but why doesn't it say, Police officers who commit crimes shall be removed and prosecuted? Why doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is that a fair question to put to this witness, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you have expected, in your position, with your length of service, that the order issued by Mico Stanisic would have said these criminals within the police shall be removed and criminal reports filed against them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what's so odd about that. He ordered that we should remove those who had strayed, so to speak. And in spite of my best intentions to focus on your question, I still find it a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's do it one more time, shall we. Again. The order simply says those who commit crimes shall be dismissed or suspended from the service and placed at the disposal of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Your Honour, the order was not interpreted completely. It also says, Take the legally prescribed measures. So that should be included also. In your binder, sir, that's in tab 14. So look at the order before you reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me what the number of the order is and we'll have it up. Not the tab number, what's the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D58.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.
