Let's read 1: "Legal measures to be taken against all members the MUP who have committed criminal acts (other than political and verbal offences) before or since the beginning of the war, in other words, the formation of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they should be removed from our order, dismissed, and made available to the Army of the Serbian Republic." So the legal measures to be taken, and if you say that's a misreading, are that they shall be removed, dismissed, and made available to the army. Where does it say there "and criminal proceedings will be instituted"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are narrowing the area covered by the legal measures. Police officers act according to a legal act, and these are the legal measures referred to. The minister couldn't put a detailed description here as to all the things that should be done, but the police knew that. It was prescribed in the law. And criminal proceedings would be carried out at the same time, in parallel with the disciplinary procedure. I don't see anything here that isn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So it is your understanding and you say it would be every police officer's understanding that the legal measures are not simply throwing them out of the police and giving them to the army but also taking criminal proceedings? You say that's absolutely clear from that order, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. These are two different processes, disciplinary proceedings. For example, a policeman commits a your murder, he is automatically suspended --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm sorry, because, again, time is running out. I -- my question was simply: Do you say that any officer reading that order would realise that legal measures encompassed criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was at all trained, he would understand this. But it wouldn't be the police officer but his superior officer who would initiate the disciplinary and the criminal proceedings. And the police officer would simply participate in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, as I say, I want to move on. You were asked about the documents 1D56 and 1D55 about the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said, if I can find it -- that's right. We better have that up, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: ID -- have we got that up? 1D56.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the ministry should immediately be informed of the existence of possible wild prison, camps, et cetera, or treatment of prisoners of war, et cetera. And you said this, that: "We had nothing to do with the camps." Now, were you -- you were aware by then, weren't you, that - this is the 17th of August and that's what prompted all these requests from the ministry - that camps were being run by the police and had nothing to do with the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a leading question because something that has not yet been established is being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the witness said in chief, Your Honours, if you recall, that he had seen the television footage in relation to the Prijedor camps, Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you knew by then, by the 17th of August, that camps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When? Witness saw this picture? That's the basis for the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see the television footage aired around the 6th of August of the camps in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, definitely not. At that time, we could not watch TV regularly but only from time to time. We would get news programmes occasionally. I can't remember at what period that image kept being shown on both the Republika Srpska TV and the federal TV. It's still being shown to this day. So I couldn't tell you the date, but my knowledge about this stems from the first collegium meeting in Belgrade when this was discussed. And when I saw those images, I understood that this was what they had been talking about. But I cannot remember what period of time it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You are talk about the meeting on the 11th of July when Zupljanin explained about the camps that they were running; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's misleading. Zupljanin in -- this document does not say that running by the police at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You know, I really don't want to have to go back to each document, but I will. If there's any dispute that what Zupljanin is saying is the army rounded up people and they were left to the police to look after these people in camps; is that disputed? Is that disputed that's what he said at this meeting? Right. No, I hear it's not disputed. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the 17th of August, were you aware of the Susica camp run by police officers, by the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first hear about that then? In your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall for certain when I heard about it. There were many events. In 1992, yes, but I can't recall what month, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think it would have been fair to ask who ran the Susica camp and who was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It is -- I just want understand -- for the Trial Chamber to understand with you -- from you, Mr. Borovcanin, it's still your case, is it still what you assert, that police officers, the MUP, had nothing whatsoever to do with the running of detention camps, and they were all run by the military? Is that what you want the Trial Chamber to hear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, yes. The army was in charge of the camps. There's no doubt about that. We only provided security occasionally, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to turn to another topic, please, very quickly. You told us that you were in charge of uniformed police and had nothing to do with crime investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the uniformed police, okay, yes. I was in charge of them, but the largest part of the work was done by the crime prevention department. We were engaged in other operative work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's what you told us yesterday and to this is what I'm querying. You've been shown a large number of documents today relating to crime investigation and crime prosecutions and the like. And you've given your opinion and said you were aware of them. Why, when you were in charge of the uniformed police and did not deal with the crime, the investigation department, are you suddenly able to talk about all these matters that you were shown by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, let me try to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Shortly, please, we've got, I think, by my reckoning, 15 minutes, if we're lucky.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of your question, let me say we were not able to deal with crime investigations of that kind, especially as the police was frequently engaged in combat at the front lines. The ground was not covered, and we could barely manage to carry out our regular work and responsibilities. That's why we didn't deal with that kind of work in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but -- all right. Actually I didn't -- I think this is more argument than anything else. So can I deal with some other matters, please. Well, I'm asked to go back to -- the person in charge of Susica camp, Mr. Cvijetic wants me to put to you and perhaps you knew this, was a man called Dragan Nikolic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that Nikolic was a member of the police? This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, I just -- I'll have to -- all right. You were asked a number of questions about the investigations, I say, for which you gave various answers, so I want to put some further ones to you. When a potential crime, including a war crime, became known to the police, where was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every public security station there is a crimes register, in other words, a book in which one enters, under the different serial numbers in the different columns, the type of crime and its characteristics, the time of commission, possibly the perpetrators, and all pertinent data.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would this include cases in which a perpetrator is unknown or has left the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would -- any crime would be registered, whether the perpetrator is known or unknown. That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would the potential crime be logged in the crime register even if the police hasn't finished their full investigation into the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who knows about police work --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would have been logged. There is no dilemma there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would there ever be an instance where the police would not record a potential crime in the crime register?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something is not registered, then it didn't exist. There may have been such instances, but not that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, that's what -- something you said earlier. You wouldn't be aware of it, unless you knew from other sources, if it hadn't been recorded, would you? So someone deliberately doesn't enter a crime into the register, then you would have no knowing -- no way of knowing whether a crime had occurred and not been registered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not exactly so. Any information, even if it is post festini [as interpreted], would be registered. Even a year later. Now, regards to your question, whether people deliberately failed to register or log something, that is speculation as far as I'm concerned. I don't know. I cannot say. Individuals might have done that, but it is something that should not have happened. I don't see that any professional policeman would have withheld any information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, when RS MUP or CSB inspectors visited the SJBs, they would review the crime registers, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. They would review all the registers maintained in the stations. They would inspect all the information contained there and any abuses of power and everything that such inspection reviews presuppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Given what you know about what was happening to the non-Serb population in your CSB area, would it surprise you if crime registers showed no crimes at all committed against Muslims or Croats during this period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this, in addition to the crime register, the ministry also sent forms to be filled about committed war crimes. We didn't have that before the war because no such need existed before the war because it was a new phenomenon produced by the war. So an additional document were these questionnaires where such war crimes would be documented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll go back to the original question. Would you be surprised if crime registers for any of the stations within your area of responsibility, the CSB Romanija Birac, contained no entries at all during 1992 for crimes committed against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if there had been such crimes and they were not registered. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, on this aspect, you were shown this criminal complaint in respect of this incident in December of 1992 from Vogosca, the seven Muslims who were shot by the Serb perpetrator. You said this was a heinous crime. Was it one that was very notorious within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was a heinous crime. Now, how do you mean was it notorious in Sarajevo? What part of Sarajevo are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean well known that this incident had happened, attracting publicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not every day that such a crime happens. That's one thing. Secondly, I don't know how publicised it was, how known it was. That is something I cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, I did -- I left the question of camps, but I just need to ask a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I just wanted to alert you that it's 3.43 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether or not you agree that they were, if the police were running camps, they would be obliged, would they not, to maintain basic standards of living and the like?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is incorporated in the question: "If the police were running the camps." That is hypothetical. Before that, it should have been cleared --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just deal with it very simply. If any police chief set up a camp, a detention facility, would that be something that he would be obliged to support -- to report to his superior in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no such case. And God forbid had any been set up, this would have been the first information that would have reached the MUP. But I do not know of a single case of the MUP having set up such a place, organised it, disbanded it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not reached the MUP. Would the SJB chief be obliged to report this to his superior? Yes or no? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I referred to the instructions about urgent interim and ongoing reporting, and everything is spelled out in so many words in that instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you don't want to answer the question. All right. Finally, it was put to you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, it is not that I do not wish to reply to the question, because it is understood. In the instructions, all the instances of reporting by the person in charge of a particular station to the MUP are precisely defined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, this is the final question. You were asked about listening to the tape and interview, the intercept, and you were given the transcript between Stanisic and a man said to be Zupljanin. You said you recognised the voice of Stanisic. Would you have said that you recognised the voice of Stanisic even with the transcript if you had not done so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have recognised his voice. We spoke on the telephone many times, and I would be really remised to say that I cannot recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you listened to the intercepts yesterday -- on Sunday, is it right you did not have any transcripts given to you? You listened to them without the assistance of a transcript?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, namely, I did not have a transcript. But there is no dispute about anything there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. So we -- Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. So we are not adjourning yet. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the usher -- you are now released and the usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to thank you for an extremely correct and fair treatment of myself on the part of all your associates from the moment I landed at the airport up to this very moment. I offer my gratitude to all of them and to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, about the one document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exhibit 1931, yes. Your Honours, it was removed from the 65 ter list in 2008 as part of this great culling. Because I instructed Ms. Bosnjakovic to clean up, if I can, some of the writing that was on the exhibit list, also cleaned up, was the warning to me, this that had been removed. So I forgot about it, so it's entirely my fault. Your Honours, you will remember it's all about Bratunac war crimes and the like. It couldn't be more relevant. The witness was able to speak to it. There was no objection to its admission. The Defence knew it, and I'm sorry about that. But please can we have it as an exhibit, still?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we more or less thought of that explanation, which is more or less evident. We have a slight problem with the fact that one of our in-home investigators, not to say Sherlock Holmes, saw that this document was very recently uploaded. So someone on your team must have realised, if I understand well the system, that it was not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was aware, originally. What I said was, when I got -- Your Honours will recall, you mentioned that normally the 10.000 list, which is clear that it's new on our 65 ter list, is marked in red. And I explained to Your Honour yesterday, when I was explaining that it was not on our 65 ter list, that there were markings on this particular document. There's been a change this week between Mr. Smith and Ms. Bosnjakovic. But some of the markings were other notes to me about those documents. So I said, Just remove the whole lot before we send it out because of the internal reminder. But also removed, by an error, was the fact that this was not on our 65 ter -- had been removed from our 65 ter list, so I knew about it. But I forgot when I was going through them because I had an uncoloured version because -- and because the number was 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say, I have a little trouble with Legal Officers spending time which, in my view, could be better spent on other things. I know that in double-checking the document admission, if there's not an objection or an argument, then, with the greatest of respect, we do spend, as Your Honours have said, quite rightly, a lot of time on this. There are -- there were problems with the way that we organised our case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, let me just say, I strongly disagree with what you said about our team members and how they should act and shouldn't act. They are doing a great job, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I am sorry, I didn't mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I must bring this discussion to a close as everyone would be aware that we are dependent on the interpreters to facilitate our work, and we are now trenching on our time. So we will take the adjournment now and resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, just for the record, the Defence for Zupljanin fully adopts submission expressed in Stanisic Defence response dated and filed on 23rd February, 2010, with regard to the 65 ter. Just for the record. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of February, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
